summary.text: For every prime \(p\), the only admissible integers at most \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and arbitrarily large primes \(p\ge100\) gives \((\log p)^{1/2}>2=a(p)\), contradicting the proposed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(m)=\{q:q\text{ is prime and }q\mid m\}
\]
denote the set of prime factors of a positive integer \(m\). The sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and }P(k)\subseteq P(n)\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]
In all comparisons below, the integer \(a(n)\) is regarded as a real number.

The key observation is that \(a(p)\) is constant on the primes.

**Lemma.** If \(p\) is prime, then \(a(p)=2\).

**Proof.** Since \(p\) is prime, its set of prime factors is exactly
\[
P(p)=\{p\}.
\]
We determine all integers \(k\) with \(1\le k\le p\) and \(P(k)\subseteq P(p)\).

First, \(k=1\) is admissible because \(1\) has no prime factors, so
\(P(1)=\varnothing\subseteq\{p\}\). Also, \(k=p\) is admissible because
\(P(p)=\{p\}\).

Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) and \(P(k)\subseteq\{p\}\). There are two cases.

* If \(k=1\), it is one of the two integers already listed.
* If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). Thus \(q\in P(k)\), and the inclusion \(P(k)\subseteq\{p\}\) forces \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\). Since \(k\ge1\), divisibility gives \(p\le k\), while by hypothesis \(k\le p\). Therefore \(k=p\).

Thus the admissible set is exactly \(\{1,p\}\), which has two elements. Hence \(a(p)=2\). \(\square\)

We next record an elementary logarithmic estimate that will make the conjectured lower bound strictly larger than \(2\). We claim that
\[
4<\log 100.
\]
Indeed, the standard estimate \(e<3\) gives
\[
e^4<3^4=81<100.
\]
The exponential and logarithm are strictly increasing on the relevant positive arguments, and \(\log(e^4)=4\), so taking logarithms yields
\[
4<\log 100.
\]
Consequently, for every integer \(p\ge100\), monotonicity of the logarithm gives
\[
4<\log 100\le\log p.
\]
Both sides are positive, so taking square roots, which is strictly increasing on nonnegative real numbers, gives
\[
2=\sqrt4<\sqrt{\log p}=(\log p)^{1/2}.
\]
Thus every prime \(p\ge100\) satisfies the two incompatible-looking facts
\[
a(p)=2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(\log p)^{1/2}>2.
\]

We now negate the conjecture by contradiction. Suppose the proposed eventual lower bound were true. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be a natural number \(N\) such that for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}\le a(n).
\]
Since \(1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12\), this says
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n)
\qquad(n\ge N).
\]

There are arbitrarily large primes, so choose a prime
\[
p\ge\max\{N,100\}.
\]
In particular, \(p\ge N\), and the assumed eventual bound applied at \(n=p\) yields
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
By the lemma, \(a(p)=2\), and hence
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le2.
\]
On the other hand, because \(p\ge100\), the logarithmic estimate above gives
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}.
\]
Combining these inequalities would give \(2<2\), a contradiction.

Therefore, already for the single choice \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), no threshold \(N\) can make the proposed inequality hold for every \(n\ge N\): every threshold is exceeded by a prime \(p\) for which \(a(p)=2\) while \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\). Hence the conjecture is false.
